claim: The ventral rhombomere 1 of the embryonic mouse (Mus musculus) brainstem produces neuronal precursors that can differentiate into either inhibitory GABAergic or excitatory glutamatergic neurons important for the control of behaviour.
source: The ventral rhombomere 1 of the embryonic mouse (Mus musculus) brainstem produces neuronal precursors that can differentiate into either inhibitory GABAergic or excitatory glutamatergic neurons important for the control of behaviour.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a background fact about the biological system under study.

claim: TFs Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are required for adopting the GABAergic neuronal identity and inhibiting the glutamatergic identity.
source: TFs Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are required for adopting the GABAergic neuronal identity and inhibiting the glutamatergic identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work and data presented in the manuscript showing loss-of-function effects.

claim: The Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 genes are activated by highly similar mechanisms, with connections to regional patterning, neurogenic cell cycle exit and general course of neuronal differentiation.
source: Our results show that the Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 genes are activated by highly similar mechanisms, with connections to regional patterning, neurogenic cell cycle exit and general course of neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on chromatin accessibility and TF binding analyses presented in the results.

claim: After activation, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are linked by auto- and cross-regulation as well as regulatory interactions with TFs of the glutamatergic branch.
source: After activation, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are linked by auto- and cross-regulation as well as regulatory interactions with TFs of the glutamatergic branch.
evidence: This finding is supported by footprinting and CUT&Tag data showing TF binding at selector gene regulatory elements.

claim: Unlike genes specific to the glutamatergic branch, the genes expressed in GABAergic neurons appear to be under combinatorial control of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3.
source: Unlike genes specific to the glutamatergic branch, the genes expressed in GABAergic neurons appear to be under combinatorial control of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3.
evidence: This is based on target gene analysis showing overlap of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 targets in GABAergic neurons.

claim: The anterior brainstem is a complex neuronal mosaic controlling mood, motivation and movement.
source: The anterior brainstem is a complex neuronal mosaic controlling mood, motivation and movement.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: An important source of these neurons is the ventrolateral rhombomere 1 (r1), where GABA- and glutamatergic neuron precursors are generated from a neuroepithelial region expressing a homeodomain (HD) transcription factor (TF) Nkx6-1 (Lahti et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2012).
source: An important source of these neurons is the ventrolateral rhombomere 1 (r1), where GABA- and glutamatergic neuron precursors are generated from a neuroepithelial region expressing a homeodomain (HD) transcription factor (TF) Nkx6-1 (Lahti et al., 2016; Waite et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rV2 precursors give rise to GABAergic neurons in the posterior Substantia Nigra pars reticulata, Ventral Tegmental Area, Rostromedial Tegmental Nucleus, and Ventral Tegmental Nucleus, all important for various aspects of behavioural control (Lahti et al., 2016; Morello et al., 2020a).
source: The rV2 precursors give rise to GABAergic neurons in the posterior Substantia Nigra pars reticulata, Ventral Tegmental Area, Rostromedial Tegmental Nucleus, and Ventral Tegmental Nucleus, all important for various aspects of behavioural control (Lahti et al., 2016; Morello et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A failure in the differentiation of the rV2 GABAergic neurons in the embryonic mouse brain, caused by mutation of the Tal1 gene, results in robust behavioural changes in postnatal mice, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, hypersensitivity to reward and learning deficits (Morello et al., 2020a).
source: A failure in the differentiation of the rV2 GABAergic neurons in the embryonic mouse brain, caused by mutation of the Tal1 gene, results in robust behavioural changes in postnatal mice, including hyperactivity, impulsivity, hypersensitivity to reward and learning deficits (Morello et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The Nkx6-1 positive proliferative progenitors of rV2 give rise to postmitotic V2b-like GABAergic precursors expressing selector genes Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, and V2a-like glutamatergic precursors expressing Vsx1 and Vsx2 (Achim et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2009; Muroyama et al., 2005).
source: The Nkx6-1 positive proliferative progenitors of rV2 give rise to postmitotic V2b-like GABAergic precursors expressing selector genes Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, and V2a-like glutamatergic precursors expressing Vsx1 and Vsx2 (Achim et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2009; Muroyama et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the absence of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 function, differentiation of all the rV2 precursors is directed to glutamatergic neuron types (Achim et al., 2012; Lahti et al., 2016).
source: In the absence of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 function, differentiation of all the rV2 precursors is directed to glutamatergic neuron types (Achim et al., 2012; Lahti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 also retain their expression in the mature GABAergic neurons.
source: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 also retain their expression in the mature GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about these transcription factors.

claim: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 TFs operate as fate selectors, possibly responsible for both the induction and maintenance of the GABAergic identity in the anterior ventrolateral brainstem.
source: Thus, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 TFs operate as fate selectors, possibly responsible for both the induction and maintenance of the GABAergic identity in the anterior ventrolateral brainstem.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns and loss-of-function data.

claim: The rV2 cells were arranged on pseudotemporal axes representing differentiating GABAergic or glutamatergic lineages.
source: We found that the rV2 cells were arranged on pseudotemporal axes representing differentiating GABAergic or glutamatergic lineages (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data analysis and visualization shown in Figure 1.

claim: The GABAergic and glutamatergic selector TF genes (Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx1, Vsx2, Lhx4) were strongly expressed in the post-mitotic precursors at lineage bifurcation point and at the start of the lineage branches.
source: The GABAergic and glutamatergic selector TF genes (Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx1, Vsx2, Lhx4) were strongly expressed in the post-mitotic precursors at lineage bifurcation point and at the start of the lineage branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq expression data shown in the figure.

claim: Open chromatin features largely reflected the gene expression in the ventral r1 and allowed placing the developing rV2 neurons in cell groups and in a pseudotemporal order.
source: In conclusion, open chromatin features largely reflected the gene expression in the ventral r1 and allowed placing the developing rV2 neurons in cell groups and in a pseudotemporal order.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integration of scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq data.

claim: The Tal1 locus, ±50 kb of the TSS, contains genes Stil, Tal1, Pdzk1ip1, and Cyp4x1 and 20 scATAC-seq features.
source: The Tal1 locus, ±50 kb of the TSS, contains genes Stil, Tal1, Pdzk1ip1, and Cyp4x1 and 20 scATAC-seq features (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and visualization in Figure 2A.

claim: Accessibility of 15 out of the 107 features in the TAD containing the Tal1 gene was linked to the Tal1 expression (p-value <0.05).
source: Accessibility of 15 out of the 107 features in the TAD containing the Tal1 gene was linked to the Tal1 expression (p-value <0.05) (Supplementary file 3, Tal1 cCREs).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of feature-to-gene linkage.

claim: The gain in the accessibility of Tal1 cCREs at +0.7 and +40 kb correlated temporally with the up-regulation of Tal1 mRNA levels, strongly increasing in the earliest GABAergic precursors (GA1) and maintained at a lower level in the more mature GABAergic precursor groups (GA2–GA6).
source: For example, the gain in the accessibility of Tal1 cCREs at +0.7 and +40 kb correlated temporally with the up-regulation of Tal1 mRNA levels, strongly increasing in the earliest GABAergic precursors (GA1) and maintained at a lower level in the more mature GABAergic precursor groups (GA2–GA6), as well as Pdzk1ip1 mRNA expression, increasing transiently in the earliest GABAergic precursors (GA1) (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of chromatin accessibility and gene expression data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The identified Tal1 promoter feature (Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE) contains Tal1 midbrain and hindbrain-spinal cord enhancers characterized earlier (Bockamp et al., 1997; Sinclair et al., 1999).
source: Notably, the identified Tal1 promoter feature (Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE) contains Tal1 midbrain and hindbrain-spinal cord enhancers characterized earlier (Bockamp et al., 1997; Sinclair et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers cited in the literature.

claim: The Tal1 +40 kb cCRE corresponds to the previously characterized enhancer region driving expression in the midbrain and hindbrain (Ogilvy et al., 2007).
source: The Tal1 +40 kb cCRE corresponds to the previously characterized enhancer region driving expression in the midbrain and hindbrain (Ogilvy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously characterized enhancer.

claim: Enhancers at –3.8 and +15.1/16/16.4 kb of Tal1 have been shown to drive Tal1 expression in haematopoietic stem cells and erythrocytes (Göttgens et al., 2004; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
source: Enhancers at –3.8 and +15.1/16/16.4 kb of Tal1 have been shown to drive Tal1 expression in haematopoietic stem cells and erythrocytes (Göttgens et al., 2004; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claim: Two Gata2 cCREs, at –3.7 and +0 kb, are located in the proximal regulatory and promoter regions, which have been earlier shown to function as Gata2 mid- and hindbrain expression enhancers (Nozawa et al., 2009).
source: Of these, two Gata2 cCREs, at –3.7 and +0 kb, are located in the proximal regulatory and promoter regions, which have been earlier shown to function as Gata2 mid- and hindbrain expression enhancers (Nozawa et al., 2009), as well as critical Gata2 autoregulation elements in haematopoietic cells (Kobayashi-Osaki et al., 2005; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claim: An intronic Gata2 cCRE at +11.6 kb may mediate the regulation of Gata2 expression in the spinal cord V2 interneurons by Gata2–Tal1 co-binding (Joshi et al., 2009).
source: We also identified an intronic Gata2 cCRE at +11.6 kb that may mediate the regulation of Gata2 expression in the spinal cord V2 interneurons by Gata2–Tal1 co-binding (Joshi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with a previous study.

claim: The Gata2 +22, +25.3, and +32.8 kb cCREs were accessible in the early precursors, before the opening of the Gata2 –3.7 kb cCRE in GA1 and Gata2 +0 kb cCRE in GA3–GA6.
source: The Gata2 +22, +25.3, and +32.8 kb cCREs were accessible in the early precursors, before the opening of the Gata2 –3.7 kb cCRE in GA1 and Gata2 +0 kb cCRE in GA3–GA6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data.

claim: The Gata3 +0.6 and +2.2 kb and the five upstream cCREs locate within the previously identified Gata3 CNS enhancer region (Lakshmanan et al., 1999).
source: The Gata3 +0.6 and +2.2 kb and the five upstream cCREs locate within the previously identified Gata3 CNS enhancer region (Lakshmanan et al., 1999), and two of those also match Gata3 lens expression enhancers (Martynova et al., 2018; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claim: The Gata3 +11.1 kb cCRE corresponds to the Gata3 proximal enhancer driving expression in PNS regions (Lieuw et al., 1997).
source: The Gata3 +11.1 kb cCRE corresponds to the Gata3 proximal enhancer driving expression in PNS regions (Lieuw et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a previously characterized enhancer.

claim: The Gata3 +17.2 kb cCRE is located in the introns 3 and 4 of the Gata3 gene and may have enhancer activity in spinal cord V2b interneurons (Joshi et al., 2009; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
source: The Gata3 +17.2 kb cCRE is located in the introns 3 and 4 of the Gata3 gene and may have enhancer activity in spinal cord V2b interneurons (Joshi et al., 2009; Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with a previous study.

claim: The accessibility of the cCREs of the GABAergic selector TF genes changed with different kinetics during neuronal differentiation.
source: Importantly, the accessibility of the cCREs of the GABAergic selector TF genes changed with different kinetics during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data.

claim: The accessibility of Tal1 +15.1, +16, +23, and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs was robustly detected before and at the onset of GABAergic differentiation and declined thereafter.
source: For example, the accessibility of Tal1 +15.1, +16, +23, and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs was robustly detected before and at the onset of GABAergic differentiation and declined thereafter (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Tal1 +23 kb cCRE contained two scATAC-seq peaks, having temporally different patterns of accessibility.
source: The Tal1 +23 kb cCRE contained two scATAC-seq peaks, having temporally different patterns of accessibility.
evidence: This is based on detailed analysis of chromatin accessibility data.

claim: The 3′ end of the Tal1 +23 kb feature contains binding sites of Nkx6-1 and Ascl1 that are expressed in the rV2 neuronal progenitors, while the 5′ end contains TF-binding sites of Insm1 and Tal1 TFs that are activated in early precursors.
source: Detailed feature analysis indicated that the 3′ end of this feature contains binding sites of Nkx6-1 and Ascl1 that are expressed in the rV2 neuronal progenitors, while the 5′ end contains TF-binding sites of Insm1 and Tal1 TFs that are activated in early precursors (described below, see Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on footprinting analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The accessibility of the Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE largely reflected the Tal1 mRNA expression and, unlike the early-peaking cCREs, such as Tal1 +40 kb, it was accessible also in the late GABAergic neuron precursors GA3–GA6.
source: The accessibility of the Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE largely reflected the Tal1 mRNA expression and, unlike the early-peaking cCREs, such as Tal1 +40 kb, it was accessible also in the late GABAergic neuron precursors GA3–GA6 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of chromatin accessibility and gene expression data.

claim: Distinct regulatory elements of the selector TFs may be responsible for the activation and for the maintenance of the lineage-specific expression of selector TF gene.
source: Thus, distinct regulatory elements of the selector TFs may be responsible for the activation and for the maintenance of the lineage-specific expression of selector TF gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different temporal patterns of cCRE accessibility.

claim: Vsx2 gene expression was detected in the common precursors CO1 and increased in CO2 and the glutamatergic precursors (GL1–GL5).
source: Vsx2 gene expression was detected in the common precursors CO1 and increased in CO2 and the glutamatergic precursors (GL1–GL5) (Figure 2C, RNA expression).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At the Vsx2 locus, an intronic feature (Vsx2 +20.5 kb) and the distal features at –61 and –21.3 kb of Vsx2 TSS were opened concomitant with its expression activation, whereas accessibility of the Vsx2 promoter region (Vsx2 +1.1 kb cCRE) and +27 kb cCRE increased later in the glutamatergic precursors.
source: At the Vsx2 locus, an intronic feature (Vsx2 +20.5 kb) and the distal features at –61 and –21.3 kb of Vsx2 TSS were opened concomitant with its expression activation, whereas accessibility of the Vsx2 promoter region (Vsx2 +1.1 kb cCRE) and +27 kb cCRE increased later in the glutamatergic precursors (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of chromatin accessibility data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Vsx2 r1 cCREs at –18.7, –21.3, +1.1, and +20.5 kb match previously characterized enhancers of Vsx2 expression in photoreceptor cells and retinal bipolar neurons and also contain putative autoregulatory Vsx2-binding sites occupied in developing spinal cord motor neuron and interneuron lineages.
source: The information about the enhancers of Vsx2 brain expression is scarce, but our Vsx2 r1 cCREs at –18.7, –21.3, +1.1, and +20.5 kb match previously characterized enhancers of Vsx2 expression in photoreceptor cells and retinal bipolar neurons and also contain putative autoregulatory Vsx2-binding sites occupied in developing spinal cord motor neuron and interneuron lineages (Supplementary file 4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously characterized enhancers.

claim: Odds ratios per chromosome were highest for exons and lowest for introns, odds ratios for features were between these two.
source: Systematically, odds ratios per chromosome were highest for exons and lowest for introns, odds ratios for features were between these two.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of sequence conservation.

claim: All of the odds ratios showed a significant difference from what is expected if there was no relationship between the nucleotides within features and conservation (p = <2.20e−16, Fisher's exact test, Supplementary file 5, sheet per chromosome).
source: All of the odds ratios showed a significant difference from what is expected if there was no relationship between the nucleotides within features and conservation (p = <2.20e−16, Fisher's exact test, Supplementary file 5, sheet per chromosome).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of sequence conservation.

claim: The conservation of chromatin features is consistent with a putative role as regulatory sites.
source: The conservation of chromatin features is consistent with a putative role as regulatory sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation analysis.

claim: The previously characterized enhancers, and especially the nervous system expression enhancers of Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 mostly are found within the ATAC features identified here (63.6–100% of gene enhancers overlapping with scATAC-seq features, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
source: Furthermore, literature research revealed that the previously characterized enhancers, and especially the nervous system expression enhancers of Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 mostly are found within the ATAC features identified here (63.6–100% of gene enhancers overlapping with scATAC-seq features, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of identified features with previously characterized enhancers.

claim: Both Tal1 and Vsx2 cCREs contain conserved binding sites of Kr-like TFs, bHLH TFs, E2A, Ebf, E2F, NF-1, Pbx, and Sox TF families, and various HD TFs.
source: We observed both common and distinct patterns of TF binding in the cCREs of Tal1 and Vsx2 in the rV2 common precursors and early GABA- and glutamatergic cells. Both Tal1 and Vsx2 cCREs contain conserved binding sites of Kr-like TFs, bHLH TFs, E2A, Ebf, E2F, NF-1, Pbx, and Sox TF families, and various HD TFs (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is based on footprinting analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Four Sox TFs are expressed in early rV2 lineage cells (Sox2, Sox3, Sox4, and Sox11), which all may compete for the same binding sites in Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE or Vsx2 –61 kb cCRE.
source: For example, four Sox TFs are expressed in early rV2 lineage cells (Sox2, Sox3, Sox4, and Sox11), which all may compete for the same binding sites in Tal1 +0.7 kb cCRE or Vsx2 –61 kb cCRE (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a speculation based on expression data and binding site analysis.

claim: Identification of the common regulators of GABAergic fate selectors revealed 21 TFs in CO1–2 and 22 TFs in the GA1–2 cell groups.
source: To further understand the mechanisms of the activation of lineage-specific selector expression, we asked which TFs commonly and specifically regulate the GABAergic selector TF genes Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3. Identification of the common regulators of GABAergic fate selectors revealed 21 TFs in CO1–2 and 22 TFs in the GA1–2 cell groups (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TF footprints at selector gene cCREs.

claim: The common regulators between the stages are overlapping partially, with the TFs associated with the neurogenic cell cycle exit predominant in the common precursors (CO) and the postmitotic differentiation and the autoregulation network TFs showing activity later in the GABAergic precursors.
source: Interestingly, the common regulators between the stages are overlapping partially, with the TFs associated with the neurogenic cell cycle exit predominant in the common precursors (CO) and the postmitotic differentiation and the autoregulation network TFs showing activity later in the GABAergic precursors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identity and timing of TF activity.

claim: 12 TFs, including Ascl1, E2f1, Nkx6-1, and Vsx1 may regulate both GABA- and glutamatergic selectors in the CO1–2 cell group.
source: We next asked which upstream regulators are common to both rV2 GABAergic (Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3) and glutamatergic (Vsx1 and Vsx2) fate selector genes. We identified 12 TFs, including Ascl1, E2f1, Nkx6-1, and Vsx1 that may regulate both GABA- and glutamatergic selectors in the CO1–2 cell group (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2F, genes indicated in bold).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TF footprints at selector gene cCREs.

claim: The distinct regulators of GABA- and glutamatergic fate selectors, aside from the lineage-specific autoregulatory functions of the selectors themselves, include Lhx1 and En2 in the GABAergic sublineage and Lhx4, Shox2, and Nhlh2 regulating Vsx2 expression in the glutamatergic lineage.
source: The distinct regulators of GABA- and glutamatergic fate selectors, aside from the lineage-specific autoregulatory functions of the selectors themselves, include Lhx1 and En2 in the GABAergic sublineage (Lhx1-binding Tal1 +0.7 kb feature, Figure 3B), and Lhx4, Shox2, and Nhlh2 regulating Vsx2 expression in the glutamatergic lineage (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TF footprints at selector gene cCREs.

claim: Footprints at Nkx6-1 TFBS were detected in the cCREs of all selectors in common precursors, but after onset of differentiation, they become restricted to the cCREs of Vsx2 and Vsx1 in the glutamatergic cells.
source: Footprints at Nkx6-1 TFBS were detected in the cCREs of all selectors in common precursors, but after onset of differentiation, they become restricted to the cCREs of Vsx2 and Vsx1 in the glutamatergic cells.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of TF footprints.

claim: The Vsx2 –68.8 kb cCRE contains conserved GATA TF-binding sites.
source: Interestingly, the Vsx2 –68.8 kb cCRE contains conserved GATA TF-binding sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on binding site analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Vsx1- and Vsx2-binding sites were found in the cCREs of Gata2 and Gata3, suggesting a mutual cross-regulation between the GABA- and glutamatergic selector genes.
source: Conversely, Vsx1- and Vsx2-binding sites were found in the cCREs of Gata2 and Gata3, suggesting a mutual cross-regulation between the GABA- and glutamatergic selector genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of binding sites.

claim: Putative Vsx1-binding sites were detected in all three GABAergic fate selector genes, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, in the rV2 common precursors.
source: Putative Vsx1-binding sites were detected in all three GABAergic fate selector genes, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, in the rV2 common precursors (Figure 3E, CO, CO1–2).
evidence: This is based on binding site analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Ascl1 and Neurog2 TFBS are found at the cCREs of both Tal1 and Vsx2.
source: The proneural bHLH TFs appeared to contribute to the activation of the selector genes. Ascl1 and Neurog2 TFBS are found at the cCREs of both Tal1 (Figure 3C, D) and Vsx2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is based on binding site analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Neurog1 TFBS was bound at Vsx2 +20.5 and –61 kb cCREs in the rV2 common precursors.
source: In addition, Neurog1 TFBS was bound at Vsx2 +20.5 and –61 kb cCREs in the rV2 common precursors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: This is based on footprinting analysis shown in the figure.

claim: Several cell cycle-associated TFs may also contribute to the regulation of selector gene expression, including Sox2, Sox21, Insm1, Ebf1, Ebf3, and E2f1.
source: Interestingly, several cell cycle-associated TFs may also contribute to the regulation of selector gene expression. Those include Sox2, Sox21, Insm1, Ebf1, Ebf3, and E2f1.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the presence of binding sites and known TF functions.

claim: E2f1 binds Tal1 cCREs +0.7 and +7 kb and is strongly expressed in the CO1–2, the common precursors of rV2 GABA- and glutamatergic cells.
source: E2f1, and Ebf1–3-binding sites are located within the GC-rich areas (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E). E2f1 binds Tal1 cCREs +0.7 and +7 kb and is strongly expressed in the CO1–2, the common precursors of rV2 GABA- and glutamatergic cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on footprinting and expression data shown in the figure.

claim: The expression of E2f1 declines after differentiation, while Ebf1–3 are expressed in common precursors (CO1–2) and maintained in differentiating neurons of both GABA- and glutamatergic sublineages (GA1–2 and GL1–2).
source: The expression of E2f1 declines after differentiation, while Ebf1–3 are expressed in common precursors (CO1–2) and maintained in differentiating neurons of both GABA- and glutamatergic sublineages (GA1–2 and GL1–2) (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is based on expression data shown in the figures.

claim: The scATAC-seq feature analysis suggested that Ebf1–3 TFs interact with Tal1 cCREs as well as Gata2 cCREs in both GABA- and glutamatergic cells.
source: Interestingly, the scATAC-seq feature analysis suggested that Ebf1–3 TFs interact with Tal1 cCREs as well as Gata2 cCREs in both GABA- and glutamatergic cells (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on feature linkage analysis.

claim: The binding of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 at the Tal1 cCREs was supported by CUT&Tag.
source: In addition to the footprint analysis, we analysed chromatin interactions of Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Vsx2, Ebf1, and Insm1 in the E12.5 r1 by CUT&Tag (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 5). The binding of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 at the Tal1 cCREs was supported by CUT&Tag (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), consistent with the autoregulatory activity of the GABAergic fate selector genes.
evidence: This is based on CUT&Tag data shown in the figures.

claim: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 binding was detected at the Tal1 +23 kb cCRE, where scATAC-footprinting did not indicate binding at conserved sites.
source: In addition to the Tal1 +0.7 and +40 kb cCREs, we detected Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 binding at the Tal1 +23 kb cCRE, where scATAC-footprinting did not indicate binding at conserved sites (Figure 3A, C).
evidence: This is based on CUT&Tag data compared with footprinting data.

claim: Insm1 footprints were found in Tal1 cCREs –3.8 and +23 kb, while Insm1 CUT&Tag peaks were found at Tal1 +7, and +23 kb cCREs.
source: The DNA binding of Insm1 and Ebf1 was also partially confirmed by CUT&Tag. Insm1 footprints were found in Tal1 cCREs –3.8 and +23 kb, while Insm1 CUT&Tag peaks were found at Tal1 +7, and +23 kb cCREs (Figure 3A, CUT&Tag Insm1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of footprinting and CUT&Tag data.

claim: scATAC-footprint was found at the conserved Ebf1 TFBS in Tal1 +77.4 kb cCRE and, by CUT&Tag, Ebf1 was found to interact with Tal1 +23 kb and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs.
source: scATAC-footprint was found at the conserved Ebf1 TFBS in Tal1 +77.4 kb cCRE and, by CUT&Tag, Ebf1 was found to interact with Tal1 +23 kb and Tal1 +40 kb cCREs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on comparison of footprinting and CUT&Tag data.

claim: Overall comparison of TF binding detected by scATAC-seq footprinting and by CUT&Tag indicates strong bias towards the same features.
source: Overall comparison of TF binding detected by scATAC-seq footprinting and by CUT&Tag indicates strong bias towards the same features (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two methods.

claim: In our analysis, equivalent percentages range from 5.3% to 25.9%, depending on the TF.
source: Earlier reports of corroborations between Cut&Run and footprinting have shown 9% (Lmx1b) and 30.5% (Pet1) of footprints having overlapping Cut&Run peak (Eastman et al., 2025). In our analysis, equivalent percentages range from 5.3% to 25.9%, depending on the TF.
evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of footprinting and CUT&Tag data.

claim: An analysis of footprint positions in relation to CUT&Tag peaks indicates clear tendency of having most footprints towards the centre of the peaks.
source: Additionally, an analysis of footprint positions in relation to CUT&Tag peaks indicates clear tendency of having most footprints towards the centre of the peaks (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), further validating eligibility of CUT&Tag and footprinting as corroborating methods.
evidence: This is based on spatial analysis of footprints within CUT&Tag peaks.

claim: The expression of Insm1, Sox4, E2f1, Ebf1, and Tead2 mRNA was detected in the ventricular zone of the ventrolateral r1 at E12.5 and overlapped with Tal1 mRNA expression in the cells located close to the ventricular zone.
source: The expression of Insm1, Sox4, E2f1, Ebf1, and Tead2 mRNA was detected in the ventricular zone of the ventrolateral r1 at E12.5 and overlapped with Tal1 mRNA expression in the cells located close to the ventricular zone (Figure 4A–C, arrowheads in a4, a7, b4, b7, c4).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The maximum intensity of Insm1, E2f1, and Tead2 probe signal is detected slightly closer to the ventricular surface (VS) than that of Tal1.
source: We quantified the intensity of the fluorescence signal of each RNAscope probe along the apical-to-basal axis of the neuroepithelium (Figure 4D–F, arrow), and found that the maximum intensity of Insm1, E2f1, and Tead2 probe signal is detected slightly closer to the ventricular surface (VS) than that of Tal1 (Figure 4D, E).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The expression of Ebf1 followed the pattern of expression of Tal1 closely, but was expressed at slightly higher levels earlier.
source: The expression of Ebf1 followed the pattern of expression of Tal1 closely, but was expressed at slightly higher levels earlier (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The maximum intensity of Sox4 mRNA was detected in the cells at a more basal position in the neuroepithelium, where the differentiated neurons reside.
source: The maximum intensity of Sox4 mRNA (Figure 4A, a5–a7, and D) was detected in the cells at a more basal position in the neuroepithelium, where the differentiated neurons reside.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The expression patterns observed along the apical–basal axis in the E12.5 r1 neuroepithelium matched with the expression patterns detected by scRNA-seq in the respective cell groups along the pseudotemporal axis.
source: The expression patterns observed along the apical–basal axis in the E12.5 r1 neuroepithelium (Figure 4D–F) matched with the expression patterns detected by scRNA-seq in the respective cell groups along the pseudotemporal axis (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is based on comparison of in situ hybridization and scRNA-seq data.

claim: Insm1, Sox4, E2f1, Ebf1, and Tead2 are expressed in the early rV2 precursors, including the Tal1-expressing GABAergic neuron precursors.
source: In conclusion, Insm1, Sox4, E2f1, Ebf1, and Tead2 are expressed in the early rV2 precursors, including the Tal1-expressing GABAergic neuron precursors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the in situ hybridization data.

claim: The expression of these TFs precedes the expression of Tal1 on the differentiation axis, consistent with a putative role in the initiation of Tal1 gene expression.
source: The expression of these TFs precedes the expression of Tal1 on the differentiation axis, consistent with a putative role in the initiation of Tal1 gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal expression patterns.

claim: Accessible genomic regions in rV2 progenitor and precursor cells are enriched in Sox, NeuroD1 and Nfia/b/x TF-binding motifs.
source: Consistent with the footprint analysis in cCREs, ChromVAR analysis indicated that accessible genomic regions in rV2 progenitor and precursor cells are enriched in Sox, NeuroD1 and Nfia/b/x TF-binding motifs (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on ChromVAR analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Sox, NeuroD1 and Nfia/b/x TFs have been suggested to regulate temporal dynamics of gene expression in mouse neural tube (Sagner et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024) and the cell cycle exit of early dopaminergic neuron progenitors (Lahti et al., 2025).
source: Those TFs have been suggested to regulate temporal dynamics of gene expression in mouse neural tube (Sagner et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024) and the cell cycle exit of early dopaminergic neuron progenitors (Lahti et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nhlh1/2, NeuroD2, Bhlhe22, Ebf1–3, Pou3f4, and Lhx5 motifs are accessible in common precursors, shortly preceding the gain of accessibility in Gata2/3 and Tal1 motifs in GABAergic neurons.
source: In addition, we found Nhlh1/2, NeuroD2, Bhlhe22, Ebf1–3, Pou3f4, and Lhx5 motifs are accessible in common precursors, shortly preceding the gain of accessibility in Gata2/3 and Tal1 motifs in GABAergic neurons (Figure 5A, square).
evidence: This is based on ChromVAR analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many of the TFs with footprints in selector gene cCREs had a genome-wide activity pattern consistent with a regulatory function.
source: In conclusion, many of the TFs with footprints in selector gene cCREs had a genome-wide activity pattern consistent with a regulatory function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChromVAR analysis.

claim: For Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 TFs, the accessibility at most of their TFBSs closely follows the TF RNA expression.
source: We also analysed the activity of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 in the rV2 neurons more closely. For those TFs, the accessibility at most of their TFBSs closely follows the TF RNA expression (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of motif accessibility and gene expression data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Of the Tal1 TFBSs, the activity pattern of the TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B motif was most specific to the GABAergic lineage, similar to the Gata2 and Gata3 TFBSs.
source: Interestingly, there are three TFBS motifs of Tal1 in the HOCOMOCO v12 resource. Of these Tal1 TFBSs, the activity pattern of the TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B motif (Figure 5C, TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B) was most specific to the GABAergic lineage, similar to the Gata2 and Gata3 TFBSs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on ChromVAR analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B is a 19-bp motif that consists of an E-box and GATA sequence and is likely bound by heteromeric Gata2–Tal1 TF complex, but may also be bound by Gata2, Gata3, or Tal1 TFs separately.
source: The TAL1.H12CORE.0.P.B is a 19-bp motif that consists of an E-box and GATA sequence and is likely bound by heteromeric Gata2–Tal1 TF complex, but may also be bound by Gata2, Gata3, or Tal1 TFs separately.
evidence: This is an inference based on the motif composition.

claim: 3948 target genes of Tal1, 780 target genes of Gata2, and 721 target genes of Gata3 were identified.
source: Using the combined evidence of TF footprints, TFBS conservation and in vivo CUT&Tag experiments (Figure 6A), we identified 3948 target genes of Tal1, 780 target genes of Gata2, and 721 target genes of Gata3 (Figure 6B, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on integrated analysis of multiple data types.

claim: About half of the identified target genes are differentially expressed in GABA- or glutamatergic neurons.
source: About half of the identified target genes are differentially expressed in GABA- or glutamatergic neurons (differential expression between the GA1–2 and GL1–2 groups with p-value <0.01 in Wilcoxon's test).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis.

claim: Most of the identified target genes of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are lowly expressed in the GABA- and glutamatergic neurons, with only 30% of the genes being expressed above RNA avg(exp) >0.5 (log1p) in GA1–2 or GL1–2 cell groups.
source: However, most of the identified target genes of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are lowly expressed in the GABA- and glutamatergic neurons, with only 30% of the genes being expressed above RNA avg(exp) >0.5 (log1p) in GA1–2 or GL1–2 cell groups (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on expression analysis of target genes.

claim: Tal1 target genes are expressed in both GABA- and glutamatergic neurons.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) showed that Tal1 target genes are expressed in both GABA- and glutamatergic neurons (Figure 6C), while Gata2 and Gata3 target genes are overexpressed in GABAergic over glutamatergic precursors (Figure 6H, M).
evidence: This is based on GSEA shown in Figure 6.

claim: Gata2 and Gata3 target genes are overexpressed in GABAergic over glutamatergic precursors.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) showed that Tal1 target genes are expressed in both GABA- and glutamatergic neurons (Figure 6C), while Gata2 and Gata3 target genes are overexpressed in GABAergic over glutamatergic precursors (Figure 6H, M).
evidence: This is based on GSEA shown in Figure 6.

claim: The expression variability in rV2 cell groups was higher for proximal feature-linked Tal1 target genes than for distal feature-linked genes.
source: The calculation of expression variability of the target genes, stratified by the distance to closest selector-bound linked feature, showed that the expression variability in rV2 cell groups was higher for proximal feature-linked Tal1 target genes than for distal feature-linked genes (Figure 6F, K, P).
evidence: This is based on analysis of expression variability shown in Figure 6.

claim: Regardless of the large amounts of potential distal regulatory elements for many targets, the target genes with proximal selector TF-bound features (0–5 kb) show the most cell-type-specific patterns.
source: Thus, regardless of the large amounts of potential distal regulatory elements for many targets, the target genes with proximal selector TF-bound features (0–5 kb) show the most cell-type-specific patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression variability analysis.

claim: A few cell-type-specific genes also appeared to be regulated by distal features, for example at >50 kb from the TSS (St18, Nkx6-1, Nhlh1) or 5–50 kb from TSS (Zfpm1, Lmo1) in the case of Tal1 targets.
source: However, a few cell-type-specific genes also appeared to be regulated by distal features, for example at >50 kb from the TSS (St18, Nkx6-1, Nhlh1) or 5–50 kb from TSS (Zfpm1, Lmo1) in the case of Tal1 targets (Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is based on analysis of target genes and their regulatory features.

claim: Cell type associations of the highly expressed target genes revealed clear enrichment of inhibitory interneuron markers among the Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 target genes.
source: Finally, we also investigated cell type associations of the highly expressed target genes (exp >0.5 (log1p) in GA1–2 or GL1–2 cell groups) by calculating scores against CellMarker 2024 database (Chen et al., 2013; Hu et al., 2023), revealing clear enrichment of inhibitory interneuron markers among the Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 target genes (Figure 6G, L, Q).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis against the CellMarker database.

claim: No common target genes were found among the glutamatergic neuron-specific genes.
source: Finally, we analysed the overlap of the cell-type-specific target gene lists, aiming to find genes regulated by all the GABAergic fate selectors (common target genes) or by any selector TF specifically. No common target genes were found among the glutamatergic neuron-specific genes (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is based on analysis of target gene overlap.

claim: The genes commonly regulated by Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are exclusively overexpressed in the GABAergic lineage and contain genes comprising the autoregulatory and GATA co-factor networks (Gata2, Tal1, Zfpm1, Lmo1).
source: The genes commonly regulated by Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 are exclusively overexpressed in the GABAergic lineage and contain genes comprising the autoregulatory and GATA co-factor networks (Gata2, Tal1, Zfpm1, Lmo1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of common target genes.

claim: The GABAergic phenotype (Gad1, Gad2, Slc32a1) is regulated by Gata2 and Gata3.
source: The GABAergic phenotype (Gad1, Gad2, Slc32a1) is regulated by Gata2 and Gata3 (Supplementary file 8, Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on target gene analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Tal1 seems to be involved in the activation or modulation of Notch signalling pathway genes (Pdzk1ip1, Hes5).
source: Tal1 seems to be involved in the activation or modulation of Notch signalling pathway genes (Pdzk1ip1, Hes5).
evidence: This is an inference based on target gene analysis.

claim: Tal1 also interacts with genes specific to rV2 glutamatergic cells (Lhx4, Nkx6-1), possibly repressing their expression in the developing GABAergic precursors.
source: Interestingly, Tal1 also interacts with genes specific to rV2 glutamatergic cells (Lhx4, Nkx6-1), possibly repressing their expression in the developing GABAergic precursors.
evidence: This is a speculation based on target gene analysis.

claim: As Tal1 is expressed already in the common precursors of rV2 lineage, the possibility of the activation of Lhx4 by Tal1 is not excluded.
source: However, as Tal1 is expressed already in the common precursors of rV2 lineage, the possibility of the activation of Lhx4 by Tal1 is not excluded.
evidence: This is a speculation based on expression timing.

claim: Gata3 may repress the Vsx2 expression in the GABAergic cells, while Vsx2 may repress Lmo1 in glutamatergic cells, establishing the initiated cell type-specific gene expression programmes.
source: We also suggest the cross-regulation of GABA- and glutamatergic selector genes in the developing rV2 neuronal precursors: Gata3 may repress the Vsx2 expression in the GABAergic cells, while Vsx2 may repress Lmo1 in glutamatergic cells, establishing the initiated cell type-specific gene expression programmes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculation based on target gene analysis and expression patterns.

claim: Nkx6-1 directly regulates the spatial expression pattern of the selector TFs important for acquisition of GABAergic and glutamatergic neuron phenotypes.
source: In ventrolateral r1, the Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, and Vsx2 TFs are activated in the region where the proliferative progenitor cells express the HD TF Nkx6-1 (Achim et al., 2012; Lahti et al., 2016). Our result suggests that Nkx6-1 directly regulates the spatial expression pattern of the selector TFs important for acquisition of GABAergic and glutamatergic neuron phenotypes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial correlation of Nkx6-1 expression and selector TF activation, and footprinting data showing Nkx6-1 binding at selector gene cCREs.

claim: Nkx6-1 is not sufficient for selector TF expression, which is activated only when the proliferative progenitor cells exit the cell cycle and give rise to postmitotic precursors.
source: Nkx6-1 is not sufficient for selector TF expression, which is activated only when the proliferative progenitor cells exit the cell cycle and give rise to postmitotic precursors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal expression patterns of Nkx6-1 and selector TFs.

claim: TFs E2f1, Ebf1, and Insm1 temporally control the selector TFs and connect their expression to cell cycle exit.
source: Our results suggest that TFs E2f1, Ebf1, and Insm1 temporally control the selector TFs and connect their expression to cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal expression patterns and binding site analysis.

claim: E2f1 is best known for its function as a positive regulator of cell cycle progression.
source: E2f1 is best known for its function as a positive regulator of cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: There is evidence for a more complex role for E2f1 in cell cycle regulation, where the effect of E2f1 is dependent on its level of expression, low levels promoting cell cycle progression but elevated levels cell cycle exit (Radhakrishnan et al., 2004; Shats et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2007).
source: However, there also is evidence for a more complex role for E2f1 in cell cycle regulation. It has been suggested that the effect of E2f1 is dependent on its level of expression, low levels promoting cell cycle progression but elevated levels cell cycle exit (Radhakrishnan et al., 2004; Shats et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: E2f1 is expressed at a low level in the proliferative progenitors, and its expression peaks concomitant to cell cycle exit.
source: Our results are consistent with this observation. E2f1 is expressed at a low level in the proliferative progenitors, and its expression peaks concomitant to cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is based on expression data from in situ hybridization and scRNA-seq.

claim: Ebf1 and Insm1 have earlier been associated with cell cycle exit and delamination of neuronal progenitors, as well as differentiation and migration of post-mitotic precursors (Faedo et al., 2017; Garcia-Dominguez et al., 2003; Monaghan et al., 2017; Tavano et al., 2018).
source: Also, Ebf1 and Insm1 have earlier been associated with cell cycle exit and delamination of neuronal progenitors, as well as differentiation and migration of post-mitotic precursors (Faedo et al., 2017; Garcia-Dominguez et al., 2003; Monaghan et al., 2017; Tavano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanisms that guide cell cycle exit and other cell biological events of neurogenesis may also contribute to activation of neuronal selector TF expression and adoption of the neuronal phenotype.
source: Thus, the mechanisms that guide cell cycle exit and other cell biological events of neurogenesis may also contribute to activation of neuronal selector TF expression and adoption of the neuronal phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation of cell cycle exit and selector TF activation.

claim: Positive feedback loops are commonly found in the gene regulatory networks involving developmental selector TFs.
source: Positive feedback loops are commonly found in the gene regulatory networks involving developmental selector TFs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The positive feedback loops can ensure stable cell fate decisions.
source: The positive feedback loops can ensure stable cell fate decisions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Tal and Gata TFs have been shown to autoregulate their own gene expression in haematopoietic cells (Wilson et al., 2010).
source: Tal and Gata TFs have been shown to autoregulate their own gene expression in haematopoietic cells (Wilson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Autoregulation is a prominent feature of the control of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 expression in the developing brain.
source: Our results suggest that autoregulation is also a prominent feature of the control of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 expression in the developing brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the footprinting and CUT&Tag data showing binding of these TFs at their own regulatory elements.

claim: Gata2 and Gata3 were shown to be dispensable for the initial induction of the Tal1 expression, but required for its maintenance (Lahti et al., 2016).
source: This is also supported by loss-of-function studies in the mice, where Gata2 and Gata3 were shown to be dispensable for the initial induction of the Tal1 expression, but required for its maintenance (Lahti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tal1 is required for the maintenance of Gata2 and Gata3 expression in the embryonic r1.
source: Reciprocally, Tal1 is required for the maintenance of Gata2 and Gata3 expression in the embryonic r1.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact, likely based on previous studies.

claim: At maintaining their expression by positive feedback, Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 appear to work together, potentially as a physical complex involving Lmo1 (Ono et al., 1998).
source: At maintaining their expression by positive feedback, these TFs appear to work together, potentially as a physical complex involving Lmo1 (Ono et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the co-regulation patterns and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 also interact with the genes of glutamatergic lineage-specific TFs, such as Vsx2 and Lhx4, expressed in the glutamatergic precursors.
source: In addition to the positive cross-regulation of Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3, these TFs also interact with the genes of glutamatergic lineage-specific TFs, such as Vsx2 and Lhx4, expressed in the glutamatergic precursors.
evidence: This is based on target gene analysis showing Vsx2 and Lhx4 as targets of GABAergic selector TFs.

claim: Negative feedback allowing cross-repression between the Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Lmo1 network, and Vsx2 in the cells where both alternative fate selectors are expressed would ensure robust patterns of selector TF expression.
source: We envision negative feedback allowing cross-repression between the Tal1, Gata2, Gata3, Lmo1 network, and Vsx2 in the cells where both alternative fate selectors are expressed. Auto- and cross-regulation would ensure robust patterns of selector TF expression, also after the initial inputs for their activation have ceased.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the regulatory interactions identified.

claim: According to scRNA-seq and earlier studies in the developing spinal cord V2 domain (Francius et al., 2016; Karunaratne et al., 2002), the time of co-expression of Gata2/3 and Vsx1/2 is short.
source: TFs often have context-dependent activating or repressive effects on their targets, and our data on chromatin occupancy cannot distinguish between the two possible outcomes. However, according to our scRNA-seq and earlier studies in the developing spinal cord V2 domain (Francius et al., 2016; Karunaratne et al., 2002), the time of co-expression of Gata2/3 and Vsx1/2 is short.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq data and citations to previous studies.

claim: In the rV2, Vsx1 is expressed in the rV2 common precursors, where Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 expression is still low.
source: In the rV2, Vsx1 is expressed in the rV2 common precursors, where Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 expression is still low.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-seq expression data.

claim: Vsx1 has been shown to repress the expression of Tal1 in the zebrafish spinal cord V2a interneurons (Zhang et al., 2020).
source: Furthermore, Vsx1 has been shown to repress the expression of Tal1 in the zebrafish spinal cord V2a interneurons (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tal1 overexpression results in reduction of Vsx2 expression in mouse ventral spinal cord V2a/V2b interneurons (Muroyama et al., 2005).
source: Tal1 overexpression results in reduction of Vsx2 expression in mouse ventral spinal cord V2a/V2b interneurons (Muroyama et al., 2005) and the overexpression of Gata3 also results in the reduction of the number of Vsx2 expressing cells in the chicken ventral spinal cord (Karunaratne et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The overexpression of Gata3 results in the reduction of the number of Vsx2 expressing cells in the chicken ventral spinal cord (Karunaratne et al., 2002).
source: Tal1 overexpression results in reduction of Vsx2 expression in mouse ventral spinal cord V2a/V2b interneurons (Muroyama et al., 2005) and the overexpression of Gata3 also results in the reduction of the number of Vsx2 expressing cells in the chicken ventral spinal cord (Karunaratne et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: A combinatory function of the selector TFs is important for adopting a GABAergic identity.
source: In addition to establishing cell-type-specific patterns of selector TF expression, the selector TFs are thought to be responsible for realization of neuronal identities. Our results show that a combinatory function of the selector TFs is important for adopting a GABAergic identity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the target gene analysis showing combinatorial regulation.

claim: Similar fate transformations observed in Tal1 and Gata2/Gata3 mutant embryos support the combinatory function of the selector TFs (Lahti et al., 2016).
source: This is supported by similar fate transformations observed in Tal1 and Gata2/Gata3 mutant embryos (Lahti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The activity of Tal1 is not as clearly biased towards genes expressed in the GABAergic branch as are the genes regulated by Gata2 and Gata3.
source: Importantly, our results here also highlight differences between Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 target genes. Most prominently, the activity of Tal1 is not as clearly biased towards genes expressed in the GABAergic branch as are the genes regulated by Gata2 and Gata3.
evidence: This is based on GSEA showing different enrichment patterns for Tal1 vs Gata2/Gata3 targets.

claim: The Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 selector TFs appear to regulate not only GABAergic subtype-specific genes, but also genes expressed more broadly.
source: In general, the Tal1, Gata2, and Gata3 selector TFs appear to regulate not only GABAergic subtype-specific genes, but also genes expressed more broadly.
evidence: This is based on target gene analysis showing targets expressed in both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons.

claim: The function of the fate selectors is not restricted to regulation of the neuronal subtype properties such as the neurotransmitter phenotype, but they also participate in enabling the overall cellular function.
source: This suggests that the function of the fate selectors is not restricted to regulation of the neuronal subtype properties such as the neurotransmitter phenotype, but they also participate in enabling the overall cellular function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the broad range of target genes.

claim: The anterior brainstem is an important centre for behavioural control, and many of the behavioural disorders have a developmental basis.
source: In addition to addressing principles of cell differentiation, our work may also contribute to understanding of neuropsychiatric traits and disorders. The anterior brainstem is an important centre for behavioural control, and many of the behavioural disorders have a developmental basis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In mice, a failure in the development of Tal1-dependent neurons results in severe ADHD-like behavioural changes (Morello et al., 2020b).
source: We have shown that, in mice, a failure in the development of Tal1-dependent neurons results in severe ADHD-like behavioural changes (Morello et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: It is possible that variants in the genomic regions important for gene regulation during brainstem neuron differentiation can lead to altered brain development and predisposition to neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: It is therefore possible that variants in the genomic regions important for gene regulation during brainstem neuron differentiation can lead to altered brain development and predisposition to neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study and the known link between brainstem development and behavior.
